name: Simulated Nature and City Walks (15-min videos, mood and restoration)
description:
Faithful replication of Brancato, Van Hedger, Berman & Van Hedger (2022), "Simulated nature walks improve psychological well-being along a natural to urban continuum", Journal of Environmental Psychology 82, 101779. The four 15-minute walk videos are the authors' own stimuli from OSF xgkvn (posted without a licence; the authors cut them from YouTube walking videos, whose links are credited in the page). They are used with credit and this template will be taken down if the authors or the video owners object.

What participants do: after consent they rate how happy, sad, calm, anxious and lonely they feel right now (0–100 sliders, not at all – extremely). They are randomly assigned to one of four simulated walks along a natural-to-urban continuum: a pine forest along the Metolius River (Oregon), a farmed wheat field, a tree-lined neighbourhood in Boston's Beacon Hill in the rain, or a bustling Midtown Manhattan / Times Square walk. The 15-minute video plays in the page with sound (pause allowed, no skipping); Continue appears only when it has ended. Then the five feelings again, PANAS (20 words, 1–5), perceived restorativeness of the video (9 items: being away, extent, fascination), Mental Bandwidth Scale (7 items: self-awareness, daydreaming, planning), Nature Relatedness Scale (21 items), TIPI (10 items, 1–7), UCLA Loneliness (8 items), age, gender, and a short description of what they saw and heard (attention check), followed by the original debriefing.

What the original found (abstract; 202 online participants, 4 groups): the walks influenced affect and perceived restoration differently even within the same nominal category. The pine forest walk improved happiness relative to both urban walks, whereas the farmed field walk did not; the bustling city walk decreased calmness compared to all other walks, including the tree-lined neighbourhood; daydreaming and being away differed in a graded fashion, and the farmed field walk was less fascinating than all other walks.

Data: vas_pre and vas_post = { happy, sad, calm, anxious, lonely }; walk = { condition, watched_s, pauses, completed }; panas, prs, mbs, nrs, tipi, ucla = { item: score } with the original item order; age, gender, attn. Analysis as in the paper: post − pre change per feeling and the PRS/MBS subscales compared across the four walks (one-way ANOVA with post-hoc pairwise tests, FDR-corrected).

Differences from the original study: (1) the video plays inside the survey page (split into three 5-minute parts, re-encoded to about 0.5 Mbit/s at the original 720 × 480) instead of on a separate page that gave a completion code; the last second of each 901-second video is cut; (2) the State and Trait forms of the STAI used in the original are left out because the STAI is a copyrighted instrument; (3) the letter of information is shortened and the Worker ID / payment parts are removed; (4) gender options follow the original (Female, Male, Non-binary, Other, Prefer not to say).
author: Brancato, Van Hedger, Berman & Van Hedger

elements.name: consent
elements.title: I have read the information about this study and I agree to participate.

elements.name: vas_pre
elements.title: Before we begin, please rate how you are feeling right now.
elements.description: { happy, sad, calm, anxious, lonely } on 0–100 sliders (0 = not at all, 100 = extremely); PRE_VAS_* in the open data.

elements.name: walk
elements.title: Assigned virtual walk
elements.description: { condition: 'forest' | 'field' | 'treelined' | 'city', watched_s, pauses, completed } — random assignment, as CONDIT in the open data (Pine Forest, Farm Field, Treelined Neighborhood, Bustling City). The 15-minute video plays in three 5-minute parts without seeking; Continue appears when it has ended.

elements.name: vas_post
elements.title: Please rate how you are feeling right now.
elements.description: Same five 0–100 sliders after the walk. Main outcome: post − pre change (HAPPY_DIFF … LONELY_DIFF) compared between the four walks (ANOVA / pairwise tests).

config.description: Rebuilt from Brancato, Van Hedger, Berman & Van Hedger (2022), Journal of Environmental Psychology 82:101779, with the authors' four 15-minute walk videos from OSF xgkvn. Each participant is randomly assigned to one walk (pine forest, farmed field, tree-lined neighbourhood or bustling city centre), rates five feelings on 0–100 sliders before and after, then answers PANAS, perceived restorativeness (9 items), mental bandwidth (7 items), Nature Relatedness (21 items), TIPI (10 items), UCLA Loneliness (8 items), age, gender and a short description of the video.
